hints: Compare the trees in Fig. 5.2 for the source and the founder islands, then use the two bullet points about perch diameter to link branch size to limb function.
walkthrough:
Link Vegetation to Selection Pressure**
Fig. 5.2 shows the source island has a large tree while the seven founder islands have only low shrubs. That means perch diameter is much smaller on the founder islands.

Apply the Correlation**
You are told shorter hind limbs give stability on smaller diameters, while longer limbs suit larger diameters. Lizards with shorter limbs will therefore survive better on the founder islands, so natural selection will shift the mean downward.
Final answer: Mean hind limb length will decrease.

hints: Think about what picking just one male and one female at random means - will each pair carry exactly the same alleles for limb length as the whole source population?
walkthrough:
Think About Random Founders**
Only two lizards start each new population. Random sampling like this does not capture the full allele range of the source population - this is the founder effect.

Conclude the Effect on the Mean**
By chance, some pairs will have alleles for slightly longer limbs and some for slightly shorter limbs, so the starting mean will be different on each island.
Final answer: Mean hind limb length will vary / differ between the different islands.

hints: Start by tracing each line in Fig. 5.3 from 2006 to 2009 - what happens to the source island line compared with all seven founder island lines?
Recall the names for selection that shifts a mean in one direction versus selection that keeps a mean constant around an optimum.
Check the 2006 starting points - why do the founder islands already start below the source and at different values from each other?
Go back to Fig. 5.2 to identify the new environmental pressure on the founder islands that would favour one extreme of limb length.
Build the causal chain for evolution - advantageous trait leads to survival, reproduction, passing on alleles and change in allele frequency.
walkthrough:
Describe the Founder Island Trend**
In Fig. 5.3 every founder line, islands 1 to 7, falls from 2006 to 2009. This consistent shift of the mean to one extreme is directional selection.

Describe the Source Island Trend**
The source island line stays flat and high across 2006 to 2009. Keeping the mean constant around the existing optimum is stabilising selection. The 2006 differences between islands reflect the random founder effect from (a)(ii).

Explain the Selection Pressure**
Fig. 5.2 shows founder islands have only small shrubs, so perch diameter is reduced. Short hind limbs are a selective advantage there because they give stability on thin branches.

Explain the Evolutionary Response**
Lizards with short limbs survive better and reproduce, passing on alleles for short limbs to offspring. Over generations the frequency of those alleles increases, so mean limb length falls.

Final answer: On all seven experimental islands mean hind limb length decreased; directional selection. On source island mean stayed the same; stabilising selection. Thinner perches select for short limbs which give stability and higher survival, survivors reproduce and pass on alleles for short limbs, increasing their frequency.

hints: Focus on the geography - what does living on separate islands separated by sea mean for mating between populations?
Think about why isolated populations would not stay genetically identical - consider environment, new mutations and chance changes.
Remember what must accumulate over time to turn separate populations into separate species with reproductive isolation.
walkthrough:
Establish Isolation**
This is allopatric speciation. The sea between islands geographically isolates the lizard populations, so there is no gene flow or interbreeding between islands.

Create Genetic Divergence**
Each island has different environmental conditions and selection pressures, such as perch diameter. In addition, different random mutations occur and genetic drift acts differently in each small population.

Reach Speciation**
Because genes cannot be shared, genetic differences accumulate independently. Eventually differences are so large that individuals from different islands cannot produce fertile offspring - they are reproductively isolated species.

Final answer: Allopatric speciation. Populations on different islands are geographically isolated with no gene flow. Different selection pressures / different mutations / genetic drift cause genetic differences to accumulate leading to reproductive isolation.

hints: Recall how each population started - how many alleles can just two founders carry compared with a large source population?
Think about what happens when close relatives must mate over generations in terms of homozygosity and harmful recessive alleles.
Consider how a population with little variation copes if disease, hurricane or food shortage strikes.
walkthrough:
Small Starting Gene Pool**
Each population was founded by only one pair, so it has a very small population size and low genetic diversity. There are few different alleles available for future adaptation.

Inbreeding Problem**
With so few mates, inbreeding is unavoidable. This increases homozygosity and exposes harmful recessive alleles, causing inbreeding depression, reduced fertility and weaker offspring.

Unable to Adapt**
Low variation means natural selection has little to act on if the environment changes or a disaster like a hurricane or disease arrives. The whole population may be equally vulnerable and become extinct.

Final answer: Each island has a small population with low genetic diversity / small gene pool. Inbreeding leads to high homozygosity / inbreeding depression. Lack of variation means environmental change / disaster can kill the whole population leading to extinction.
